aboutAuthor: Simon Sinek is a British-American author and motivational speaker whose 2009 TED talk on this book became one of the most-watched of all time. He advises leaders and organizations on purpose-driven leadership.

points.heading: The Golden Circle: Why, How, What
points.body: Every organization knows what it does; some know how; very few know why. Inspired leaders communicate from the inside out — starting with purpose. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it.

points.heading: The brain responds to 'why' before features
points.body: The limbic brain drives decision-making and emotion but has no capacity for language, while the neocortex handles rational analysis. When you lead with Why you speak directly to feeling — facts and features only justify decisions already made.

points.heading: Apple sells belief, not computers
points.body: Apple's message is everything-we-do-challenges-the-status-quo, and its products merely prove it. Customers who share the belief will pay a premium and queue overnight. Competitors with better specs on paper still lose the loyalty war.

points.heading: Manipulation vs. inspiration
points.body: Discounts, fear, peer pressure, and novelty all work — once. They are manipulations that erode trust and guarantee a treadmill of deeper discounts. Only genuine inspiration creates loyal customers who repeat and refer without incentives.

points.heading: The celery test keeps you honest
points.body: If you go to the store with advice from everyone, you buy everything and waste money. Filter every decision through your Why: if it doesn't serve your purpose, don't buy it. Discipline in what you refuse is what makes your signal clear.

points.heading: Loyalty follows clarity of belief
points.body: Organizations that say and do the same thing consistently attract employees and customers who believe what they believe. That cultural alignment — not compensation schemes — is what sustains great companies through hard times.

insights: Sinek's 'Why' concept draws on Simon Sinek's study of the Wright Brothers versus heavily funded rival Samuel Langley.
The TiVo paradox: most-featured product, worst customer understanding — people described what it did, not what it meant.
Sinek argues hiring for belief explains why some teams achieve 'impossible' goals together.
conclusion: Start With Why argues that lasting influence flows from purpose communicated before product. Clarify your why, filter every choice through it, and you'll attract people who believe what you believe — and they'll stick with you through anything.
